body.text: BRICS is considered as a bloc of emerging and developing countries looking for a greater voice in a world order still dominated by institutions created by the West. It began as a four-country grouping of Brazil, Russia, India and China, became BRICS when South Africa joined in 2011, and expanded substantially in the 2020s. Its members use the grouping to coordinate positions on global governance, finance, trade, development, and international security. It has no treaty comparable to that of a military alliance and no central authority that can enforce its decisions. Its main instrument is political agreement. Governments meet, negotiate a declaration and commit themselves to things they say they will do together.

That makes BRICS easy to measure. Every summit produces a document, and those documents contain commitments. The useful question is what happens to them afterwards. The leaders of the expanded grouping met in New Delhi on September 12 and 13 for the 18th BRICS summit. The declaration issued at the end of the meeting is the 18th annual declaration in the series. It contains 140 numbered paragraphs and ranges across global governance, the UN, the IMF, trade, finance, development, climate change, technology, and other areas of cooperation.

The declarations have grown more ambitious over time. The first summit, at Yekaterinburg in 2009, produced 15 commitments, according to the BRICS Research Group at the University of Toronto. Its count rises to 137 for Kazan in 2024; the Brazilian chair counted 126 commitments in the 2025 Rio declaration. The increase reflects the widening of BRICS’s agenda as the grouping has expanded and accumulated working groups, institutions and areas of cooperation.

But a longer declaration does not necessarily mean a more effective organisation. A summit can produce dozens of promises without changing what governments actually do. The BRICS Research Group has created a way to measure that distinction. It has counted commitments in the summit declarations since 2009 and, since the 2011 Sanya summit, has assessed compliance with a selection of them. Each member receives a score for whether it has fulfilled, partly fulfilled or failed to fulfil the commitments being assessed. The results allow BRICS to be compared with other major diplomatic groupings, including the G7 and G20.

The record is uneven, and India’s own line moves more sharply than the average. Compliance across the grouping reached 89 per cent after the Goa summit in 2016 and 85 per cent after Johannesburg in 2018, then fell to 40 per cent after the 2023 Johannesburg summit before recovering to 61 per cent after Kazan in 2024. The first cycle assessed across the expanded membership rather than the original five countries. India recorded full compliance after Sanya in 2011 and 95 per cent after Goa in 2016, when it held the chair; it then fell to 25 per cent after the 2023 Johannesburg summit, the lowest among the five members that year, before returning to 69 per cent after Kazan. A chair year lifts the host’s score in almost every cycle—hosting concentrates the attention of a national bureaucracy, and that shows up in the compliance table a year later. The more useful measure of BRICS, then, is not how many declarations it produces but how often its promises survive contact with governments, institutions and money.
Where the money went

Compliance scores record whether governments carried out what they announced at a summit. A second test asks what the grouping has built that outlasts the declaration announcing it. On that test, there is one institution to examine, and it publishes the hardest numbers in the record. The New Development Bank (NDB) was agreed at Fortaleza in 2014, with an initial authorised capital of $100 billion and a subscribed capital of $50 billion shared equally among the five founding members. It opened in Shanghai and made its first loans in 2016. It lends to governments and state entities for infrastructure and sustainable development, on the model of the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank. Most of what it lends is raised on the bond markets rather than drawn from the members. Its membership has widened since the founding five.

A development bank can be read on three measures, and this one publishes data for all three. The first is how much it has approved, which records ambition and political direction. The second is how much of that money has actually reached the borrower, which records the capacity of both sides to execute a project. The third is the currency it lends in, which tests the grouping’s claim to be loosening its dependence on the dollar. Approvals arrive with a press release; disbursements arrive without one. The distance between the two is the most revealing figure the bank produces.

Take approvals first. An approval means the bank’s board has cleared a loan and committed the money to a named project. The bank’s annual report for 2025, published in July, records cumulative approvals of $43.0 billion for 139 projects since lending began. Its live portfolio—counting only projects still running after cancellations and full repayments—stood at 115 projects worth $35.59 billion at the end of 2025.

China holds the largest share of that portfolio, at $9.41 billion, or 26.4 per cent. India follows at $8.86 billion, or 24.9 per cent, then Brazil at $6.69 billion and South Africa at $6.41 billion. Russia trails at $3.78 billion, its transactions having been put on hold in March 2022. The order between the two leaders changed during 2025: India was ahead at the end of 2024, with $9.65 billion against China’s $8.71 billion, and slipped behind as Indian loans were repaid and Chinese approvals grew. The five founders subscribed equal capital, so these shares record which governments brought projects to the board, not who contributed most.

Approval and delivery are separate matters, and the distance between them varies widely across the membership. Money is approved when the board clears a project, and it reaches the borrower only as the work proceeds. By the end of 2025, China had received about 75 per cent of the lending approved for it, and India 60 per cent—$7.08 billion for China against $5.30 billion for India. Brazil sits lowest, at 51 per cent. India closed much of the gap during 2025, having stood at 47 per cent a year earlier. Across the whole institution, cumulative disbursements reached $24.2 billion against $43.0 billion approved, with $21.7 billion still outstanding after repayments.

The Madhya Pradesh project takes the inquiry from finance to delivery. The NDB approved a $350 million loan towards an originally estimated $500 million project. Its evaluation rated overall performance satisfactory, but the bank’s own performance moderately unsatisfactory, identifying weaknesses in design and supervision. An evaluation of the district-roads project recorded average journeys falling from 83 to 37 minutes, and travel to a primary healthcare centre from 52 to 28 minutes. The project upgraded 1,551 km of roads against a target of 1,500, according to the bank’s Independent Evaluation Office.
The currency challenge

De-dollarisation is the loudest claim made for BRICS and the easiest to test, because the grouping’s own bank publishes both a target and the result. Its General Strategy for 2022 to 2026 undertakes to extend 30 per cent of total financing in the local currencies of member countries. The same document sets out the position it inherited: 23 per cent of cumulative approvals at the end of 2021.

For three years, almost nothing happened. At the end of 2024, the three member currencies on the books—the renminbi, the rand, and the rupee—together accounted for 24.2 per cent, against the 23 per cent inherited in 2021. Then 2025 changed the picture. Local-currency financing reached 45.9 per cent of the year’s approvals, a record for the bank, and the portfolio share rose to 29.3 per cent. The dollar fell from 65.5 per cent to 59.5 per cent in a single year. On its own measure, the bank has all but met its target, with a year of the strategy period still to run.

One qualification belongs with that figure. The target is set on financing approved during the strategy period, and the 29.3 per cent describes the whole book, so the two are not measured on identical bases. On the flow measure the bank overshot in 2025; on the stock measure it remains a few tenths of a point short.

The composition matters more than the total. The renminbi alone is 21.5 per cent of the whole book—nearly three-quarters of everything the bank lends in a member currency. The rand is 6.8 per cent. Local-currency lending, as practised, has largely meant lending in the currency of one member.

For India, the 2025 figures record a beginning rather than an arrival. Rupee financing rose from 0.3 per cent of the portfolio to 1.0 per cent. The bank approved its first rupee-denominated loan during the year: Rs.13.2 billion to a renewable-energy producer in Karnataka, along with an equity investment of up to $100 million equivalent in rupees in a government-sponsored infrastructure fund. Rupee funding has been slower. The bank aimed to issue its first rupee bond by October 2023 and did not do so. It was reported in September 2025 to be planning a debut of $400–500 million by March 2026, and its 2025 annual report described the rupee bond programme as still being finalised.

So the outcome is measurable, and the answer has two halves. The shift is real, and it arrived late—almost entirely in the final full year of a five-year plan. It also runs through one currency. The dollar still funds three-fifths of the bank founded to reduce dependence on it.

Borrowing in a currency that matches project revenues can reduce exposure to exchange-rate movements. The dollar’s continuing predominance shows how far the NDB’s portfolio remains tied to the established international financing system.

Finance ministers and central bank governors meeting under India’s chairship this month again encouraged the payments task force to work towards interoperable channels and settlement in local currencies. Interoperability means that a payment leaving a bank in India can be received by a bank in Brazil directly, through systems built to recognise each other’s instructions. Most such payments today pass through a chain of banks abroad and convert into dollars along the way. What the task force is asked to build is therefore modest in itself, since it concerns the plumbing of trade settlement rather than any common currency. The instruction is now a decade old, and two obstacles have slowed it.

The first is technical: national payment systems must agree on message formats, legal cover and supervision before they can speak to one another. The second is political, and India has stated its position plainly. External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar told an audience in London in March 2025 that India has no interest in undermining the dollar, and that the grouping holds no unified position on the question. The Reserve Bank’s then Governor, Shaktikanta Das, had said in December 2024 that de-dollarisation was not the objective. He described the steps India had taken—permitting vostro accounts and signing local-currency trade agreements—as a way to reduce the risk of depending on a single currency. A vostro account is one that a foreign bank keeps with an Indian bank, held in rupees, so that trade between the two countries can be invoiced and settled without passing through a third currency. So the bank’s second-largest borrower is also the member most explicit in disclaiming the currency shift that the bank is asked to lead. The composition of its book follows from that.
Promises that keep returning

A recurring demand that goes unmet for years is itself a measurable outcome. The oldest of them concerns the IMF. Every member of the IMF holds a quota, which is its shareholding. The quota fixes how much a country pays in, how much it may borrow when it runs into trouble, and how many votes it casts. The IMF reviews these quotas periodically, and a review can do two quite different things. It can raise every member’s quota by the same proportion, which enlarges the IMF’s resources and leaves each member’s relative weight exactly where it was. Or it can realign the shares, moving votes from countries whose economies have shrunk in relative terms towards those that have grown. Realignment is what BRICS has asked for in every declaration since 2009.

The last change to those shares came out of the IMF’s 14th review of quotas. Members approved it in 2010, and it took effect only in 2016, once the United States Congress ratified it. The 16th review concluded in December 2023 with an equiproportional increase of 50 per cent, meaning every member’s quota rose by half, and nobody’s share of the votes changed. Emerging and developing economies now produce about 60 per cent of world output and hold about 40 per cent of the voting power. Changing that requires a supermajority of 85 per cent, and the United States alone holds 17.42 per cent of the quotas, so it can block any realignment by itself. Sixteen years of asking since Yekaterinburg has produced no movement in that ratio at all.

The reserve pool tells a similar story. The Contingent Reserve Arrangement (CRA) is a standing promise among the central banks of the five founders to lend one another hard currency if one of them runs short—balance-of-payments support for a country unable to pay for its imports or service its foreign debt and needing dollars quickly. The treaty was signed at Fortaleza in 2014 and committed $100 billion. No member has ever drawn on it. The mechanism has been exercised only through test runs, rehearsals in which the central banks process a request without money changing hands.

Under the original CRA, China committed $41 billion and could access up to $20.5 billion. South Africa committed $5 billion for maximum access of $10 billion. Brazil, India, and Russia each committed $18 billion and could access the same amount. South Africa consequently obtained the highest access-to-commitment ratio, at two to one. These were contingent rights to foreign-currency support under specified conditions. The founding terms linked 70 per cent of maximum access to an arrangement with the IMF, the global crisis lender. The mechanism’s practical value, therefore, depends on its availability during financial stress, the conditions for borrowing and the speed of assistance.

The credit rating agency has fared worse still, since it never acquired so much as a founding document. A rating is a judgement on how likely a borrower is to repay, and it sets what a government pays to borrow. BRICS members have long argued that the dominant international agencies judge developing economies too harshly and raise their cost of capital as a result. The Goa Declaration of 2016 welcomed experts exploring an independent BRICS rating agency, and the idea was deferred at that summit. The Xiamen declaration the following year was silent on it, and a decade later no such agency is in operation.
Can diplomatic success be measured?

Diplomatic outcomes become measurable when the objective is specific. Assessments can record a government’s objective, the change secured in another party’s position, and the action that followed. Membership rights and implemented agreements are observable institutional outcomes.

Four distinct levels can usefully be separated from one another. Output is countable: declarations, commitments, working groups and new institutions announced. Follow-through is scoreable by the Toronto method, with the caveats its authors themselves publish. External effect is testable against a fixed list of demands—the IMF quota question is the cleanest example, because the answer is a number that either moves or stays where it is.

Cohesion adds a fourth measure, and it leaves a documentary trail. Foreign ministers meeting in New Delhi in May failed to agree on a joint communiqué, and India issued a chair’s statement instead. Counting the occasions on which a chair’s statement substitutes for consensus produces an index of internal strain that requires no interpretation. Attendance by heads of state, recorded summit by summit, supplies a second index of the same kind.

One pattern runs through the record. Where BRICS has built an institution with a balance sheet, that institution has produced results a reader can count. Where BRICS has directed its demands at the wider system, the system has not moved. The NDB has approved $43.0 billion of lending since 2016; the IMF quota shares have not shifted since 2010. These figures record what happened after each summit.
The challenge for India

India assumed its fourth chairship on January 1 and has run the year’s programme under the theme of resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability. The declaration issued on September 13 supplies the eighteenth data point in this series. Three of its features are worth recording against the baseline set out above. The first is the number of commitments it contains, which the Toronto group will count within a few months. The second is whether every member signed it without entering a reservation. The third is whether any single paragraph creates an entity with a budget, a board and an address, in the manner of Fortaleza in 2014.
The compliance score for New Delhi will not be known until the middle of 2027. That is the timetable for judging a summit.
